tagline: America's boating capital — gridlocked on land, wide open on the water.
summary: Florida is the largest recreational-boating market in the United States, a peninsula whose major coastal cities — Miami, Palm Beach, Naples–Fort Myers and Tampa Bay–Sarasota — are strung along congested coastal highways but linked by sheltered Intracoastal and open-Gulf water. The same trips that crawl on I-95 or US-41 fly clean and direct on the water. A foiling tier serves both an everyday-mobility need and one of the world's densest concentrations of high-end marine demand.
why_marine_mobility: Florida cannot be told as one city — it is a chain of coastal metros that already live on the water. South Florida's road network is chronically congested, while the parallel Intracoastal and Atlantic corridors sit underused for passenger transport. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier flies the shorter coastal legs — Palm Beach to Miami inside its 70 nm range — smooth, dry and clean, while the Quanta-LR hybrid opens the longer Gulf and cross-border trunks, from Tampa Bay down to Naples to the iconic Miami-to-Bahamas crossing, that no battery day-boat can serve.

demand_signals.label: Coastal-highway congestion
demand_signals.note: South Florida's I-95 and US-1 corridors are among the most congested in the country; parallel water routes between Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale and Miami are a direct, underused mobility alternative.

demand_signals.label: Yachting and high-net-worth density
demand_signals.note: Miami, Palm Beach and Naples form one of the densest high-net-worth marine markets in the world — major boat shows, marinas, yacht clubs and waterfront second-home communities already moving by private boat.

demand_signals.label: Established water-taxi culture
demand_signals.note: Miami and Fort Lauderdale already run water taxis and on-demand boat services, proving consumer appetite for passenger water transport on these exact corridors.

use_cases.body: Palm Beach to Miami: the ~61 nm coastal commute flown direct on Pioneer II inside its 70 nm range, bypassing the I-95 corridor with a smooth, clean, schedule-reliable water alternative.
Tampa Bay to Naples: a ~115 nm Gulf-coast trunk on Quanta-LR linking the west-coast metros — a long premium leg no all-electric day-boat can serve, opening on its hybrid range.

Miami to the Bahamas (Nassau): the iconic ~155 nm cross-Gulf-Stream crossing on Quanta-LR — a clean, fast, premium link from South Florida to the islands that today means a charter flight or a long offshore boat run.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The shorter coastal legs — Palm Beach–Miami (~61 nm) and the dense intra-metro marina hops around Biscayne Bay, Tampa Bay and the Naples–Fort Myers waterways — sit inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range at 30 knots, commercial-ready today, with low wash that suits Florida's manatee and idle-speed protection zones.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The longer trunks — Tampa Bay–Naples (~115 nm) along the Gulf coast and the ~155 nm Miami–Bahamas crossing — are Quanta-LR corridors (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), opening cross-region and cross-border legs no all-electric day-boat can reach.

signature_routes.label: Palm Beach → Miami — Atlantic coastal commute (Pioneer II)
Tampa Bay ↔ Naples — Gulf-coast long-range trunk (Quanta-LR)

transit_planning: For a transit authority, marina operator or premium charter brand: a clean water tier that doubles as everyday-mobility relief on congested coastal corridors and as a high-end charter product in the world's richest marine market. Start with the Palm Beach–Miami coastal leg and the intra-metro marina hops on Pioneer II — commercial today — then add the Gulf-coast and Bahamas trunks on Quanta-LR. The craft rides existing marina berths across all four metros, so no new shoreside infrastructure is required.
competitive_landscape: Florida already has water taxis and on-demand boat services in Miami and Fort Lauderdale, and a deep recreational-boating culture — validating consumer demand for passenger water transport on these exact corridors. What is missing is a clean, fast, foiling tier: conventional water taxis are slow, fuel-burning and high-wash, ill-suited to the state's many idle-speed and manatee protection zones. Navier's craft is faster and smoother than any incumbent water taxi, low-wash for protected waters, and the only option that scales from a short coastal commute up to the long Gulf and Bahamas trunks on one platform family.
regulatory_note: Passenger vessels are certified and inspected by the U.S. Coast Guard; on-water operation is also governed by Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, including manatee and idle-speed/slow-speed zones across the Intracoastal and bay waters where low-wash foiling is an advantage. A Miami–Bahamas leg additionally engages U.S. and Bahamian customs and immigration clearance.
seasonality: Peak demand runs the cool, dry winter season (roughly December–April) when seasonal residents and visitors arrive; the Atlantic hurricane season (June–November, peak August–October) brings storm risk and rougher water in which a stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule across choppy conditions. The sheltered Intracoastal corridors stay navigable year-round.

precedents.what: Four Seasons Lake Austin operates an N30 in live luxury-hospitality service — a direct U.S. proof point for the premium water-shuttle model Navier brings to Florida's coastal markets.
